stories.situation: The plant's first-pass defect rate had sat at about 6% for four years and was treated as the line's natural rate. Rodrigo did not believe a rate could be natural, so he started writing down which station each defect came from, by hand, every shift for six weeks.
stories.stakes: Two previous quality projects run by engineers from Mexico City had failed and the floor had stopped cooperating with them. If his failed too, the supervisors would stop giving him anything.
actions: Logged 2,400 defects by station and shift himself over six weeks, because the system recorded them only by line
Found 41% of them came from one drum-seating station on two of the three shifts
Watched that station for a full shift and saw the fixture had 4 millimetres of play that the day shift's operator compensated for by habit and the other two did not
Had the fixture shimmed for about 2,000 pesos rather than requesting the 400,000-peso replacement the engineers had proposed
Wrote the compensating habit into the station's one-page instruction so it did not depend on one person
stories.result: Defects fell from 6.1% to 4.0% over nine months, worth about 11 million pesos a year in rework and warranty. The hand-logging method was adopted at the company's two other plants. He was promoted the following year.
stories.reflection: The answer had been visible on the floor for four years and nobody had stood at the station for a whole shift. He also learned that the cheap fix is easier to get approved than the right one, and that this is sometimes a trap — he still thinks the fixture should be replaced.

stories.nickname: The night I stopped the line
stories.situation: Three weeks into being superintendent, Rodrigo stopped the night line for four hours because a batch of drums had arrived with the wrong steel gauge and he could not reach anyone with authority to confirm it. Stopping cost about 600 units.
stories.stakes: A new superintendent stopping a line on his own authority, at night, with no confirmation. If the gauge had been fine he would have cost the plant 600 units for nothing, in his first month.
actions: Measured twelve drums himself with a micrometre rather than trusting the certificate
Called the plant manager at 1 a.m., got no answer, and stopped the line anyway
Wrote the decision and his reasoning on the shift log before the plant manager arrived, so it could not be rewritten afterwards
Quarantined the whole pallet rather than sorting it, which cost more and was the right call
stories.result: The gauge was wrong by 0.3 millimetres across the batch. The supplier replaced 4,100 drums. Had they been built, the warranty exposure would have been several times the cost of the stop. The plant manager now has a standing instruction that any superintendent may stop the line on a material doubt.
stories.reflection: He was right, and he is honest that he would have been in serious trouble if he had not been, and that the certificate said the steel was correct. The standing instruction is the part that mattered, and he asked for it precisely because he does not want the next person to need luck.

stories.nickname: The test I took three times
stories.situation: Rodrigo took the GMAT three times: 560, then 590, then 610. He studied for fourteen months, mostly between 5 a.m. and 7 a.m. before the first shift. The verbal section is where he loses; he reads English technically and well and reads English arguments slowly.
stories.stakes: He had told his wife and his supervisors he was applying. After the second attempt he told them he had stopped.
actions: Took a diagnostic after the second attempt and found his verbal timing, not his comprehension, was the problem — he was finishing 8 questions short
Changed to reading one English long-form article a day out loud, which his wife suggested and which he found humiliating and effective
Booked the third attempt before he felt ready, because he had learned from the second that waiting to feel ready meant not going
Decided after the third attempt that 610 was his number and that he would apply with it rather than take a fourth
stories.result: 610, with Q44. He is applying with it. The decision to stop at three and apply anyway is the one he is least sure about and most at peace with.
stories.reflection: He believed for a year that the score was a measure of whether he was capable of the thing. He now thinks it is a measure of how fast he reads English arguments under time pressure, which is a real limitation and not the same thing. He says the first version out loud more often than the second, and knows it.

stories.situation: His father, a welder, lost the use of his right hand in an accident at work the year Rodrigo started university. The compensation was disputed for two years. Rodrigo worked nights in a tortilleria through his first two years of engineering school and sent money home.
stories.stakes: He nearly left the degree in the second year. His 7.9 average is the average of two bad years and two good ones.
actions: Moved to night classes for one semester so he could work days, then moved back
Did the compensation paperwork for his father, including two appeals, because his father could not write easily afterwards
Did not tell the university, which had a hardship fund he found out about in his final year
stories.result: His father received compensation in 2018. Rodrigo finished the degree in four years with a 7.9. His younger sister is now at the same university and he pays her fees.
stories.reflection: He understands the floor because his father worked one, and the operator who compensated for the broken fixture out of habit is his father, in his head, which is why he went and stood at that station. He has never put those two things next to each other out loud before.

stories.nickname: Six supervisors who did not want the job
stories.situation: Rodrigo inherited six supervisors, four of whom were older than him and two of whom had applied for his job. None of them would bring him a problem in his first three months.
stories.stakes: He could not run three shifts through people who would not tell him things.
actions: Worked one full shift a week on each shift's hours for two months, including the 10 p.m. start, so he saw what they saw
Gave the hand-logging defect project to the two who had applied for his job, and let them present the result to the plant manager
Stopped holding the daily meeting and started walking the line with each supervisor once a week instead
Backed one of them publicly when a Mexico City engineer blamed his shift for a fault that was the fixture's
stories.result: Both supervisors who had applied for his job are still there and one has since been promoted to a sister plant. Shift handover disputes, which used to come to him three or four times a week, now come to him about once a month.
stories.reflection: He had expected to earn it with results and it was the 10 p.m. starts that did it. He is aware that is a slow method and does not have a faster one.

goals.shortTerm: A plant manager or operations manager role at a larger manufacturer in Mexico or the southern United States, running a site rather than a floor, with responsibility for the site's cost rather than its output.
goals.longTerm: To run manufacturing operations across several plants for a company that makes physical things in Mexico, and to be the person who decides where a plant goes and how it is staffed.
goals.planB: Stay at Electrodomésticos Nava, where the plant manager role is likely in three or four years, and take the company's internal management programme instead.
goals.whyMba: He runs a floor well and has never seen a balance sheet for the plant he runs. He does not know what the site costs, what the product sells for, or how either number is decided, and he has never worked with anyone outside manufacturing. He also wants to be in a room where he is not the only person who came from the floor.
goals.whyNow: He has run three shifts for two years and the next thing at this plant is waiting for someone to retire. His sister finishes university next year, so the household no longer needs his salary every month.
